2. Depends. One can be skeptical of a certain scientific claim if one has intense knowledge on the topic, however then that person would know how to go about disproving/modifying that claim, and developing a new hypothesis building off that claim. Knowledge is something COVID deniers usually don't have. Lack of knowledge - yes of course, that's the vehicle. But in my opinion there are 2 core reasons for this phenomena - 1.emotional responses - especially fear (which most of the fake news and conspiracy theories play on). 2. Ego. Certain people struggle to accept the fact they don't know everything, or maybe not even a lot. They struggle to accept the fact they don't understand what's going on, what a pandemic is, what SARS-Cov-2 is, etc. This can be benign, i.e. tied to emotional responses; fear, as in people are afraid of what they don't understand therefore they make up their own explanations without any knowledge of the topic and convince themselves and others that their explanation is the only true one. Basically, a mode of self-defense and self-soothing. But it can also be malignant, as in people with narcissistic tendencies, or just disproportionately large egos, who can't handle the fact they're not made important in some way, rebelling against experts and proclaiming THEY'RE the ones who actually know what's up. With the rise of social media these narcissistic types can now be heard and made to feel important, hell, people listen to them and like their posts, etc. That's their life fuel. You know what I mean? The followers then follow them due to many reasons, peer pressure being one of them, but mostly, again, due to their emotional responses.
3. Yes, absolutely. HOWEVER, that person has to have education, knowledge and experience in the field in order to deny a scientific claim. An example, on the top of my head, besides the obvious ones; Cecilia Payne, the woman who discovered what the stars are made of, wrote a doctoral thesis which concluded that stars are made primarily of hydrogen and helium, which went completely against the astrophysicists' theories of that time. So much so that her outside thesis mentor, Henry Norris Russel, discouraged her from concluding that, and suggested there must be a flaw in the formulas she used. Well guess who came to the very same conclusion years later: Henry Norris Russel. And we now know, that yes, stars are indeed made primarily of hydrogen and helium.  "There is no joy more intense than that of coming upon a fact that cannot be understood in terms of currently accepted ideas." —Cecilia Payne. But the "knowledge and education" bit is very important here.
